image_description:
1. **Chart type**  
   Multi-series **line chart**, shown as three separate panels.

2. **Layout techniques**  
   - **Small multiples / faceting** by activity type:
     - Texting, phone calls and video chats
     - Exercising
     - Grooming
   - Each panel contains multiple colored lines for **age groups**.
   - No stacking.

3. **Data variables**

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Activity type (Texting/phone calls/video chats, Exercising, Grooming) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting / separate panels |
| Year (2019, 2020) | Temporal | Position on x-axis |
| Average non-work and non-school time spent per day (minutes per day) | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Age group (15–24, 25–44, 45–64, 65+) | Categorical/ordinal | Color/hue of lines and points |
| Change from 2019 to 2020 (e.g., +8 min., −5 min.) | Quantitative | Text labels at line endpoints |

1) I notice that from 2019-2020, every age is texting, calling, and video chatting more often (2-8 minutes more). I also notice that most ages are exercising more, except for 15-24 yrs (5 minutes less). Another thing I noticed is that the only age that has improved with hygiene is 15-24 yrs.
2) I wonder if everyone is going on calls and texting more often because they got used to it in the pandemic and now it is a new way of living on a daily basis. I think that the reason why most people from ages 15-24 are exercising less is that they are on technology more often, and it is taking up the time they used to exercise. I think that most people over the age of 24 are going down with their hygiene and self-care because the pandemic had a lot more stressful impact on people who are 25+ yrs.
3) This relates to my community because I have noticed the big change in technology use among people my age after covid. I also see how the change in technology can affect people wanting to text, call, etc. ALL THE TIME instead of exercising. I can relate to the hygiene thing because I see my parents getting very stressed and not having time for normal necessities. 
4) A catchy headline would be, "The Covid-19 Pandemic Changed Different Age Groups' Perspectives and Lifestyle Much More Than We Thought It Could."

1) I notice the pandemic had a huge effect on everyone but especially 15-24-year-olds. They had the most drastic changes out of all the age groups.
2) I wonder and am surprised by how little texting, calling, and video chats affected the 25-44-year-old age group. The 65+ age group went up more than the 45-64 age group as well, which to me is very surprising. 
3) As I said earlier, the pandemic had a huge effect on everyone and this graph shows just that. Lastly, what's happening in these graphs is a general survey on what people had an increase/decrease of during the pandemic. I think a good, catchy headline would be something like "How the Pandemic Has Changed Us: A Survey On Different Age Groups".

comments.raw_comment:
1. I notice that texting, phone calls, and video chatting increased for all ages, though people ages 15-24 had the highest increase, 8 minutes. I also notice that those ages 15-24 were the only ones to have a decrease in exercising, but they do still exercise the most out of all age groups. In addition,  they were the only age group to have an increase in grooming, albeit 0.4 minutes. However, compared to the decrease the other age groups had, 2. it makes me wonder what's special about this age group. Well, this age group is still going through school or college, and obviously, the elephant in the room, 2020 was the year COVID-19 struck. This means students were doing school virtually, and had more free time. So then, why did exercising decrease? Probably because all public gyms had closed, and most people would be scared to go on walks, because, well, the answer is fairly self-evident. Other age groups might be able to workout in their own home, but probably not college students. Grooming makes sense to me, since college students probably didn't have much time to take care of themselves before the pandemic, so during the pandemic, not too much changed, even a slight increase in how much they groom themselves, while other age groups didn't prioritize it as much.
3. This relates to me and my community since everyone experienced and was impacted by the pandemic, and I identify with these graphs a lot.
4. How did the pandemic change the way we use our free time?

comments.raw_comment:
1) From the graphs which are recorded from May to December 2020 vs 2019  I saw that 15-24-year-olds have increased the amount of time that they spend on texting, phone calls, and video chat while the exercising also went down for 15-24-year-olds which creates a negative correlation. For everyone older than 25 there seems to be a slight increase in phone texting, calls, and video chat but there is also an increase in exercise which creates a positive correlation. It also seems that grooming increased slightly for people from 15-24 but decreased for everyone else older.
2) I wonder how the people from 25+ increased their exercise and technology usage but their grooming decreased which creates a quite interesting correlation between the 3 factors. I wonder how this correlation will change in the future and if it will stay as a constant or will it change?
3. Over the global pandemic and certainly when the lockdown first happened people were using technology to communicate with each other. I think over time people were trying to find things to do and decided to spend time outside by taking walks and enjoying nature. It made people find other things to do than just use technology and may have created healthy habits or created even worst habits such as being stuck to the use of technology.
4.  I think the use of this graph was created to display peoples use of technology and how they took care of themselves over the pandemic
"Smart or Bad Choices"

Mr. Hibino
Statistics

1.What do you notice?
As Quarantine progressed and more people stayed home, people connected more by texting, Video calls and phone calls. Exercising decreased probably due to gyms closing and not being able to go to the gym so people worked out at home. Self care decreased due to everyone being home and not going out as much.
2. What do you wonder?
Why would older people not take care of themselves more when they have a lot more free time? Why would 15-20 year olds exercise less when they have more free time? 
I had so much more free time with covid that I would go mountain biking everyday and spend more time hanging out with friends in person outdoors (limiting chances of catching covid). Why didnt many other people take advantage of this free time.

comments.raw_comment:
Things are slowly returning to the old normal, but from the graph, we see that some of our own habits remain unchanged from during the pandemic.
The first thing I noticed was the increase in time spent on video chats and messages. What surprised me was that it had not decreased during all this time. It made sense, perhaps during the beginning of the pandemic and quarantine, when regulations were high. Back then, video chats were the only way you could communicate with your friends. But now, most students have gotten their vaccines, and the younger ones who haven’t got them don't need them to see friends. Face-to-face is now common in day-to-day life, and students already spend 6 hours a day interacting with others. After school, they hang out at the park to play basketball. They don’t exactly prefer to video chat with each other; at least, I can’t imagine why they would.
Even though we’re moving away from the secluded society which was the result of coronavirus, we have not changed our habits. Maybe it’s because we’re lazy, maybe it’s because we find that our new habits suit us better. Whatever the reason, we’re changing and developing as a society, making new adaptations as time passes. Perhaps we’ll never go back to the old normal, but instead stay at an ongoing normal.
Headline: Are We as Adaptable as Our Environment?

1. What do you notice?
The average time non-work and non-school time during the pandemic importantly decreased due to online classes and zoom meetings. However, the texting, phone calls and video chats average time increased in ages between 15-65+, the average exercising time decreased and the average grooming time only decreased in group ages 25-65+, but the group age of 15-24 remained almost the same.
2. What do you wonder?
I wonder why the average grooming time remains the same when it comes to the community with the same age as me. I wonder if it will start decreasing at some point, and I wonder why it is an outlier. I also wonder when it will start increasing again. 
3. How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because the COVID-19 pandemic affected us all in very different ways, but also in very similar ways. I noticed that my average screen time increased as well and I also noticed that my grandma started going on social media more often. I believe that we all have different ways to cope with stress that the pandemic has brought into our lives and I believe that at some point it will all be normal again. 
4. What’s going on in these graphs? Create a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.
Coronavirus: creating a lazy society?

1. I notice that texting, making phone calls, and video chatting for all ages increased. This must be due to the fact that people had more downtime and they wanted to keep themselves occupied. As well as this, I noticed that for people aged 25+, the amount of time people spent exercising also increased. However, for people aged 15-24, the amount of time exercising decreased. On the other hand, the opposite occurred for grooming. With this being said, people aged 15-24 years old spent more time grooming than people aged 25+. 
2. I wonder why the amount of time spent exercising for people aged 15-24 decreased because I felt as if I spent more time exercising during the pandemic. However, the graph shows that we spent more time on our phones instead. I also wonder why the amount of time spent grooming with people aged 25+ decreased. I would think that it would have increased considering that these people had more time to do so. 
3. This impacts me and my community because we all experienced this pandemic together and noticed changes in our daily lives. It is interesting to visualize the amount spent on everyday tasks like these. 
4. In this graph, different age groups were being studied to see how much time was spent on their phones, exercising and grooming. A catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea would be “How did COVID change the way we spend our daily lives?”

1.) What do you notice?
I noticed immediately that the amount of time spent texting or making calls or video chats steadily increased for all age groups while grooming for a majority of the older age groups plummeted. 
2.) What do you wonder? 
I wonder the reasoning for the slight decrease in exercise by the younger generation with the new options available in gyms and online while the elder population has exercised more frequently. 
3.) How does this relate to you or your community?
The pandemic-related quarantine created a drastic change in acceptable phone usage in comparison to much more in important livelihood practices, including exercise and bodily grooming. The corona virus in addition to the unhealthy practices occurring in the midst of 2020 allowed for the negative aspects that correlated with the requirement to remain home. 
4.) What is going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graphs’ main idea. 
This graph accurately portrays the average non-work/non-school time dedicated to cell phone usage, exercise, and hygiene from May 2019 to December 2020 for all ages. It is evident within that graph that texting increased across all subjects, and the fair majority of individuals failed or lessened their extent of grooming and exercise. 
Catchy headline: The Health Experts Lied

comments.raw_comment:
1. The graphs are of average free time spent per day by age. They show the difference in minutes from 2019 to 2020. The four age groups are 15-24, 25-44, 45-64, and 65+. For all age groups time spent texting, phone calls, and videos calls increased. For ages 15-24 time spent exercising decreased by five minutes, but for the other groups it increased by 4 or 5 minutes. Grooming decreased for all groups except 15-24, which had a small increase. 

2. I wonder why the time spent texting and on phone and video calls is so low. From my experience and observation people spend much longer than 15 minutes a day texting or on calls. Maybe the number is so low because it only counts communication and not social media. I also wonder why ages 15-24 exercised less. Being at home more seems to have affected exercise time of very young people differently than everyone else, according to this graph. I also wonder why ages 15-24 spent slightly more time grooming. This could be because people those ages still had to be on video calls or even in person for school, so they still maintained their appearances.

3. This impacts my community because the pandemic did affect how we spend our time. For my community the increase in time spent texting and on calls and decrease in time exercising generally applies. The almost no change in time spent grooming also makes sense because we still had to go to school.

4. “The Pandemic Redistributes Our Free Time”

Here are some of the catchy headlines that we did receive:  “Our Phones vs. Ourselves During the Pandemic” by Mariana of Jalisco, Mexico, “Covid Effects on Everyday Habits” by Ella of Grand Island, New York, “Look Where Your Time Is Going During COVID” by Adan, “Habits at Home: How Different Age Groups Changed Their Routines During the Pandemic” by Nate of Hunter College High School in New York City, "Teens in America Working Out....NOPE!" by Henry in Claremont, “Pandemic’s Effect on Free Time” by Katherine of Andover High School, Massachusetts, and "Pandemic Time: How We Spend It and How We Waste It" from Daniel in Andover, MA.

You can continue to post responses.  Please check back by Friday, September 17 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, headline shout-outs, some additional questions about the graph, and some Stat Nuggets.

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).

View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 

graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 

Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex). 

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, who texted and exercised substantially more during the pandemic, and Corey Andreasen of The Hague, Netherlands, who needs to exercise more.

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice? 
I noticed that texting, phone calls, and video chats increased the most for 15-24 year-olds and also increased in every other age group. This is because everyone was communicating by phone or video chat during quarantine. Everyone spent less time grooming because they didn’t have anywhere to be. I also noticed that 15-24 year olds were the only ones who reported a little change in time spent grooming. 

What do you wonder? 
I am curious as to why it says that 15-24 years olds are only on their phones for 15 minutes a day in this report, being 17 years old myself I can say with confidence that many people my age are spending hours on their phones, especially during quarantine. I am also curious as to why 15-24 year olds didn’t have as drastic of a decrease in time spent grooming than the other ages.


How does this relate to your community?
There were a lot of people in my community who spent time on their phones or spent time video chatting, however, a lot of my friends and family also spent the time doing exercises. My family, whom most would fit in the older category, would have fit in with what the graph shows us, I definitely would not.

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice? 

I notice that my age group (15-24) increased in online communication by significantly more time than other age groups. Also, my age group has decreased in exercise whereas every other age group has increased in that area. Lastly, my age group was the only group to increase in grooming, which shows how we're dedicating more time to self-care, at least in that arena. 

What do you wonder? 

I wonder why my age group increased in grooming yet decreased in exercise, as self-care usually includes both grooming and exercise -- these two factors are usually linked. Furthermore, I wonder why other age groups decreased in grooming, perhaps because they had to work even more at home whereas school time is typically constant. 

How does this relate to you and your community? 

It's interesting to see how my age group, late teens and early adults, have an increased electronics use and on the whole, are dedicating less time to self-care despite the greater amount of free time due to less homework and fewer commitments (on average). Furthermore, I feel like other age groups are more readily able to purchase goods/services, which may have led to the increase in exercise (for instance, they can buy a Peloton bike) amongst other age groups. The changes in grooming amongst other groups make sense because they don't need to look as good for work at home, but grooming in our age group is still a mystery to me. 

Catchy headline: Gen Z is truly the digital generation.

comments.raw_comment: This graph depicts the trend of certain activities in certain age groups in 2019 and 2020. I think that Covid-19 is a huge factor in many of the results. In all age groups, texting, phone calls, and video chats all increased. This is because of the lack of in-person communication that everyone had access to during quarantine. For all age groups except 15-24, exercise increased likely due to an increase in free time. For teens and young adults, however, exercising decreased. I believe this is because the use of electronic communication increased drastically more than any other group and almost replaced exercising all together. Grooming decreased in every age group except for 15-24, which honestly surprised me and I'm curious as to why this is. This relates to my life and community because as someone in the 15-24 age group, my phone usage has certainly followed the trend shown on the graph and it is a habit I'm trying to break. My title for this graph is "The Pandemic's Affect on Each Age Group's Time Usage"

comments.raw_comment: Something interesting about these graphs, is that no one seems to understand them. People in this comment section seem to think that 15-24 year olds increasing their time texting, using phone calls, and video calls, means increased time looking at social media. Beyond that people also seem to think that texting, phone calls, and video calls means increased phone usage. However, the graph is not looking at phone usage. Although phone calls do of course mean increased phone usage, this graph also looks at video chats and texting. Which is interesting, because video calls aren’t even primary done on phones generally, rather they are usually done on computers. Of course texting is primarily done on phones, but we can’t simply conclude that the extra time that 15-24 year olds spent on texting, phone calls, and video calls is only including these things on phones.

1. I notice that time spent on technology was the only category where everyone's time increased. 

2. - It's stressed that young people exercise a lot to stay healthy, so why aren't they exercising much during the pandemic? Is it because their only options are outdoor and outside activities? But then why wouldn't that have an effect on those older than them?

However, the times people of ages 25+ spent on grooming and exercising have undergone the opposite effects respectively. This increase in exercising is most likely due to the elderly needing to keep in shape, and the fact that 25 is not an old age whatsover; this once again leads to some of their time needing to be sacrificed, and grooming seems to be one of them. 
Title: "The Permanent Effects of the Pandemic on our Leisure Time"

comments.raw_comment:
1) All three graphs above depict similar results in that the age group is always the outlier. For example, in the first graph all of the age groups increased their time spent on their phones only by two to three minutes. Whereas the 15-24 age group increased their time spent on their phones by a whopping eight minutes. Although an increase in 8 minutes may not sound like much, comparatively speaking (with respect to the other age groups) it is a huge increase.  
2) Throughout the pandemic, technology because everyone's primary source of communication, work, etc. - so it is not unexpected that there would be an increase across the board of technology use. However, since everyone was using technology for everything it seemed like, I wonder why only the one age group increased by such a great amount. 
3) The information relates to my community and me because, throughout the pandemic, I noticed myself going on my phone and computer much more than I would have if things were normal. However, I also noticed that my parents were doing the same as well. This causes me to think: "If everyone was using technology for everything now, how is it that only my age group increased?" After thinking about this question, the results made sense. Although it is a bad habit, I feel that my age group was more likely to go on their phones while we were in online school whereas our parents, were focused on their work. 
4) How Different Generations Spent Their Time Before vs After the Pandemic

comments.raw_comment:
1) From these graphs, I noticed that the 15-24 age group had an 8-minute increase in texting, phone call, and video chat usage, but a 5-minute decrease in exercising. The two could be correlated, as people could be spending more time on their electronics, and less time being physically active. However, it was honestly surprising to see a 0.4-minute increase in time spent grooming, which does make sense, considering the greater amount of time on our hands.
2) Personally, I wonder why the 25-44, 45-64, and 65+ age groups experienced a pretty large decline in time spent grooming, but an increase in exercising. While grooming and exercising are both very necessary to personal health, I'd assume basic hygiene would be more of a priority.
3) As a person who falls between the 15-24 age group, the statistics specific to my age group relate to my own experience during quarantine. Being a remote student last year, I definitely spent more time texting and calling my friends, since we couldn't interact in-person as frequently. It was also difficult to motivate myself to go on runs, as I would regularly do during track or cross-country in previous years, but I still tried to go on walks a few times a week.
4) "Daily Life During the Pandemic: A New Age of Habit" - This headline refers to the various daily habits that have changed during the pandemic, with the relevant keywords "age" and "habit".

comments.raw_comment:
Most striking in these graphs is the large contrast between those of age 15-24 and those aged 25+.  For example, while phone usage has increased for all age groups, younger populations are being much more dramatically affected by the onset of the pandemic.

The difference is much more noticeable in the other two graphs; while older age groups are rising in exercise time and lowering time dedicated to grooming, younger populations are experiencing lower levels of exercising and higher levels of grooming.

The age group highlighted in yellow is mostly delegated to students in high school and college. Thus, there is a large factor that creates a pandemic experience dramatically different than adults.

I wonder what pressures during the pandemic are being placed on students that compel them to overperform. They are spending more time glued to their phones and less time exercising. Moreover, an increase in grooming time implies that they are still expected to look fashionable to their online peers. What tasks are they doing on their phones that drains so much of their time?

As a high schooler, I witness the physical and mental deterioration of my fellow classmates, and understanding this data could be crucial for improving the mental health of students that are experiencing increasing levels of stress during the pandemic. 

Thus, my catchy headline: Student populations are placed under unrealistic expectations for increased online presence, draining their time and mental health.

comments.raw_comment:
1) The 15-24 age group tended to stand out from the other populations somehow, with phone time increasing more dramatically, exercise decreasing where for others it decreased, and grooming increasing (if only marginally) where for others it decreased dramatically. Some of these make sense - younger generations might be more technologically up-to-date or more used to phone usage as part of normal life, and classes might interfere with time to go to the gym.

2) I do not understand why grooming increased/stayed the same, especially when all other age groups' habits decreased so dramatically. If anything, I would think that grooming would decrease, since classes were primarily virtual.

3) Increased time on the Internet and exposures to all different types of content can be debilitating for many adolescents' upbringing. In addition, increased screen time as a habit itself might affect work ethic, attention span, etc.

4) "Routine Disturbance: Pandemic Habits Across Age Groups." This title can be read two ways, since "routine" is both an adjective and a noun, and therefore describes both dramatic shifts, or disturbances, in previous lifestyles, and regular, reoccuring disturbance in the present pandemic lifestyle. While over time these changes are observable and obvious, in the moment, they are just another part of life; the "new normal" was a lack of any form of normallity.

This data set is  applicable to me and my community, simply because almost everybody I know falls under the surveyed age groups. It can be used to analyze potential trends in the future about health concerns, technology proficiency, and other factors that have changed as a result of the pandemic.

I'm curious about other potential categories.

I notice that video communication increased among all of the age groups, which makes sense considering the state of the world in the past year. I also noticed that with the exception of the first graph, the youngest group of people tend to deviate from the overall trends represented in the graph.

What do I wonder?
I wonder how they defined grooming in the third graph. I find it extremely interesting that the older groups shown in the graph all showed a steep drop in grooming time. Does this mean that there is a specific way of grooming that people between the ages of 15-24 use, and older people do not?

How does this relate to me and my community?
It relates to me because I am represented by the 15-24 age group, and I have generally seen the same trends with those around me, who are my age.

I notice that the four age groups differ in their average non-work and non-school time spent per day, and that all four age groups have been drastically affected by some factor (presumably the Covid pandemic). As a 17 year old, I notice the changes in the 15-24 age group the most: increased time spent texting/calling/video chatting, decreased time exercising, and a slight change in time spent grooming (whereas the other age groups have spent much less time grooming). While the other three age groups tend to move in a similar fashion, 15-24 year olds seem to be a bit more "independent".

I wonder how these statistics were gathered. What is the sample size and was the data collected from a representative population reflective of the country? Probably the most striking statistic is the increase in grooming time for 15-24 year olds, while an opposite change can be observed in the other age groups. Why is this? For the second graph, does the data take into account mandatory virtual PE classes?

Obviously, these statistics are very relevant to all people in the US, whose school and work have been affected by the pandemic. The first graph resonates well with my own personal experiences, as my friends and I have spent much more time video chatting compared to 2019.

A trend seen is the increase in time spent on electronics, and a decrease in the time spent exercising for people ages 15-24. Nobody cares about grooming, so we ignore the fact that the younger generation actually spent more time grooming themselves. 

Screen time went up significantly for my age range due to the focus on virtual schooling and assignments, and the primary way to connect with people was also mainly over our devices as opposed to hanging out irl. And naturally, given the opportunity, the younger generation defaulted to being lazier than before. : )

comments.raw_comment:
Did We Change For The Better Or For The Worst? 

I notice that for every age group, the time spent on texting, phone calls, and video chats increased over the course of the pandemic. The exercise results vary; people of younger ages, 15-24, decreased their exercise whereas the adults, ages 45+ increased their exercise. For the most part, grooming decreased. I wonder if this is all due to the pandemic. I also wonder if students decreased their exercise due to mental health reasons and/or being outside of school, where there is no physical education provided to them. As for the older ages, I wonder if they exercised more because most were working from home and had more free time. I wonder if people exercised because they wanted to better themselves or maybe for weight loss. I wonder if the use of technology increased because most of the population had an increase in spare time and time spent at home. Finally, I wonder if the decrease in grooming occurred because there was an increase in isolation amongst the community. As previously stated, this all relates back to the community because, at the times of May through December 2020, a worldwide pandemic occurred where everyone was forced to quarantine. Overall, the graph is displaying the changes in how we spend our free time before and during the pandemic.

comments.raw_comment: Today, this graph is displaying the average amount of time different age groups spent doing a variety activities in 2019 vs. 2020. The categories: texting, phone calls and video chats, exercising, and grooming. For the first category, every age groups minutes spent using their phone increased from 2019 until 2020, some as much as an 8 min increase. This can be attributed to one factor: COVID-19 pandemic. With kids and adults staying home all day, it's easier to find time to text, play games, etc. Also, without having the constant contact with peers in the workplace or school, people had to communicate through the internet with texting and calling. The next graph shows a decrease and increase in exercise from 2019 to 2020. The 15-24 year olds had a steady decline starting at 35 minutes of exercise a day, and ending with only 30. Given that with everyone being home you should have more free time, this statistic can only be attributed to the people actually wanting to exercise. Things like gym class and sports sort of forced exercise on this age category, and without it people chose not to exercise. The 25-44 and 65+ categories actually had a steady increase of 4 more minutes of exercise a day. The opposite occurred here, so when given more time, 25 to 65 year olds use it to exercise. The last statistic is a scary one...for since people were not leaving the house, it appears as if the time spent grooming was shortened entirely except for the 15-24 who barely spent more time.

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?

I notice how the younger generation increased their use of technology while isolated during the pandemic. At the same time exercising was less accessible for the younger age group (probably due to the decrease in sports and group activities) while the older generation had more time to exercise with remote work. Finally the younger generation spent more time grooming while the older generation decided it was less fruitful.

What do you wonder?

I wonder the impact of social media on the actions of the 15-24 year old age group. For instance, grooming could have increased due to the prevalence of a younger beauty standard proliferated by social media. 

How does this relate to you and your community?

The majority of my community fall into the youngest age group, and many of the trends can be seen through overall sentiments I have seen. This also relates to a family dynamic which is part of my community. As the older generation engages in hobbies away from technology (for my family hiking), the young became more immersed in it.

What’s going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline that captures the graphs’ main idea.

The generational pandemic.

I notice that the time spent texting, making phone calls, and video chatting went up for all age groups. For the 15-24 age group, the amount of time spent exercising went down, but it went up for all the other age groups. The time spent grooming went down for all age groups except for the 15-24 age group. Though the time spent exercising went down for the 15-24 age group, it
still remained higher than those of the age groups whose exercise time increased. For all age groups, no more than 10 minutes was added or deducted from time spent doing things. I wonder why there was so little change. I also wonder why the 15-24 age group's time spent grooming went up, since (at least in my experience) most people were less focused on grooming during the pandemic. This relates to me because a member of the 15-24 age group, I can definitely say that my time spent texting, calling, and chatting went up. However, unlike the graph shows, my time spent exercising definitely went up. My time spent grooming is probably accurately reflected by the graph.

The first graph shows how the pandemic caused a substantial increase in the use of electronics in people aged 15-24, while every other age group saw a minor increase of 2-3 minutes. This is likely due to people aged 15-24 having to attend online classes for either high school or college instead of having in person classes. The second graph saw an increase in every age group except 15-24, who saw a -5 decrease in excerise. Finally, every age group besides 15-24 saw a major decrease in time spent grooming. 

Altogether, these 3 graphs show the change in how each age group spent their time. 15-24 responded best to the change to using electronics during pandemic, as they saw the biggest change out of all 3 charts. People aged 25+ saw a minor increase in electronics but spent more time excerising and way less time grooming themselves. 15-24 did the best job of keeping themselves clean

Title: How did society's habits change during the pandemic?

In the first graph, the use of electronics including texting, phone calls and video chats increase significantly amongst all age groups compared from 2019 to 2020. In the second graph, the amount of exercise of individuals ages 15-24 decreased versus the slight increase in other age groups. In the last graph, people aged 45-64 decrease grooming significantly along with those aged 25-44 and 65+. People aged 15-24 saw no change. 

These three graphs document the habits of four different age groups before and during the pandemic. While younger people responded better to technology and communication devices, they did not respond as well to exercise but kept their grooming habits.   Other age groups did not respond as well to technology and struggled to maintain their grooming habits, but kept up their exercise regimen. 

I wonder why exercise decreased for younger people, considering they're the most physically abled group of people.

Welcome to Wednesday's line moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graphs show the average time spent per day on three activities while not in school or work spent (in minutes), by age, for May – Dec. 2019 (at the beginning of the pandemic) and for the same months in 2020.  

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and “How does this relate to you and your community?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in this graph. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included these graphs, the link to the graph's article and much more.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released on Friday, Sept. 17 with moderation on Wednesday, Sept.22.  The topic:  “normal” U.S. precipitation. 

Keep noticing and wondering.

Time Spent doing Activities in People According to 
 Age Group

I think this relates to my community and I because it shows 2019, which was life pre-Covid and then 2020 during Covid. A lot of people's lives changed a lot during this time, so it's interesting to see the different changes in activity.

comments.raw_comment: What I noticed is that there was a pretty big increase in time on the phone graph for the people from ages 15-24 and 65+. I wonder why the grooming category went down so much for 3 of the age groups. It is shocking to see how much quarantine affected people's everyday life. I think this graph is trying to point out the differences in people's lives after the pandemic hit. Personally, the pandemic had a huge effect on my motivation to be productive so I was on my phone a lot. The only thing that doesn't add up to me was the fact that I exercised more in quarantine than before and the graph shows a decrease in it. One thing that I am curious about is who contributed to the percentages. I know that random people did and not everyone experienced the same lifestyle in quarantine, but things were very different for me in quarantine than the others. In conclusion, this was a very interesting and informative graph that showed how different ages responded to the hit of the pandemic. My catchy headline is "The Different Generations through the Pandemic."

1. On these three graphs, I notice that as the time texting, phone calls and video chats increased, the time people spent "Grooming" was decreasing. If we look at the color coded lines, for yellow (age group 15-24), we can see that the time spent texting went up, and the time spent exercising went down. This is an inverse relationship. All the while, the time spent grooming stayed the same.
2. I wonder what's considered "Grooming" for this study, and how they measure it.
3. I can relate to the age group from 15 to 24. When I'm on my phone a lot, I have less time to exercise. I would say the time I spend exercising decrease for exponentially than in the graph provided. Other than that, its a carbon copy of what my community portrays. 
4. For these graphs, for the age group 15-24, at the time spent on electronics, it really affects the exercise time of this group. The grooming time had a slight increase of 0.4 minutes, but overall it stayed consistent with 40 minutes. The age group from 25 to 44 had a consistent increase in the first two graphs, (texting etc., and exercise) but had a dramatic decrease in time spent grooming. The age group from 45-64 almost replicated the age group from 25 to 44. The age of 65 and up also replicated those same patterns of 25 to 44, and 45 to 64, but more severely. I would say overall that "Texting, phone calls and video chats" affected this study greatly.
